newsitem.title: USA: Some U.S. cos seen keeping Iraq oil contracts.
newsitem.headline: Some U.S. cos seen keeping Iraq oil contracts.

text.p: At least some U.S. companies are expected to escape Baghdad's apparently politically-motivated decision to not renew oil contracts with companies whose governments have hampered Iraq's attempts to ease United Nations sanctions, diplomats and oil company sources said Thursday.
British and Japanese companies on Thursday were told by Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) that they would not get contracts, at least for the first 90-day period of the current deal.
Baghdad's decision was based on the fact that Britain and Japan had, during the December-to-June round of the "oil-for-food" deal, blocked some import contracts.

However, though the U.S. blocked far more contracts than Britain and Japan combined, at least three of the five U.S. companies which held term contracts earlier this year appeared set to have those renewed.
Under the "oil-for-food" deal, Iraq is allowed to export up to $2.14 billion of oil in two equal tranches in order to pay for food, medicine and other humanitarian supplies.

British Petroleum Co and the Anglo-Dutch Shell Group said on Thursday that SOMO decided not to renew their contracts. Mitsubishi Corp, Idemitsu Kosan Co Ltd and Cosmo Oil Ltd also were told their contracts would not be renewed, at least for the first 90-day period, which ends September 5, according to sources.

U.S. companies had not heard definitively by late Thursday about their contracts. But according to one well-informed oil trader, SOMO looked likely to renew contracts for Coastal Corp, U.S. based trading company Bayoil and Chevron Corp, but not those of Texaco Inc and Mobil Corp.

Some U.N. diplomats said Iraq's decision didn't make sense, given that Britain has had less than a dozen blocks on contracts and Japan only two, while the U.S. has put a 'hold' on more than 130 proposed import contracts.

But oil traders said Coastal and Bayoil have long-standing relationships with Iraq which stand outside politics, while Chevron appeared likely to have its contract renewed because it would bring its Iraqi crude to the U.S. West Coast, an important new market for Iraq.
Diplomats said Japan and Britain were not likely to take any retaliatory action over the commercial contracts.

Some also said they saw a good chance Iraq would change its mind about British and Japanese companies, given the amount of oil it has to bring to market over the next month in order to reach its $1 billion allowance for the first 90 days.

"I dont know if theirs is a credible explanation why they don't renew the contracts. But we don't know what they will do later -- they have a lot of oil to sell," said a diplomat on the U.N. Iraq sanctions committee.

"This may well be a storm in teacup and SOMO wakes up and says 'there is no way on Earth we are going to be able to sell the amount of oil we need to without the British and Japanese companies,'" said a Western diplomat at the U.N.
